🏴‍☠️ Tech Pirates 🌍🚀

We’re passionate tech enthusiasts exploring AI, data science, and space technology to uncover environmental trends using NASA data. We welcome enthusiastic teammates skilled in Python, machine learning, data analysis, geospatial technology, or web development. Join us to collaborate, innovate, and build meaningful solutions for a better understanding of our planet!
summary:
Trend Compass turns NASA Earth observations into an interactive space-pirate learning adventure. Players sail the Sea of Time, investigate temperature changes, estimate trends and build evidence-backed claims with guidance from First Mate Piper.

Using NASA GISTEMP v4 observations, the project answers four questions: What is changing? Where is it changing? How much is it changing? Is the change statistically significant? Theil–Sen estimates the rate of change, while the Hamed–Rao modified Mann–Kendall test evaluates significance.

Our goal is to help students and curious learners understand environmental trends through participation. Dataset sources, verification status and limitations remain visible, connecting an engaging experience with transparent scientific evidence.
details:
What we built

Trend Compass is an educational Earth science application developed by Team Tech Pirates for the “Be An Earth System Trend Detective!” challenge. It combines regional trend analysis with a playable adventure called the Sea of Time.

How it works

The temperature investigation uses NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 gridded temperature anomalies. A Python pipeline prepares the observations for regional analysis and records their source, retrieval date and SHA-256 checksums.

For a selected region, the statistical engine calculates a Theil–Sen trend estimate and uses the Hamed–Rao modified Mann–Kendall test as its primary significance test. Results include the estimated change per decade, uncertainty information and the statistical verdict.

NASA GIBS Blue Marble imagery provides geographic context. It is used as a basemap, not as an input to trend calculations.

Learning through play

In the Sea of Time prototype, players steer a ship across a chart tinted by calculated temperature trends. At an investigation beacon, they cast a net over a marked region, rotate a compass to estimate the trend, release simulated noise storms and assemble evidence receipts in Crew Court.

First Mate Piper provides short hints. Players can compare their estimate with the engine’s result, see why an unsupported claim fails and retry. The noise storms are explicitly labelled simulated teaching aids; they do not replace NASA observations or the official significance test.

Intended benefit and impact

Our intended audience is students, educators and people approaching environmental data for the first time. The project makes trend analysis something users can explore and question, rather than simply accepting a finished graph. Its intended educational impact still needs wider user testing.

Tools and technology

We used TypeScript, Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS and Phaser for the interface and game; Python and FastAPI for the backend; and NumPy, pandas, SciPy, statsmodels, pyMannKendall and xarray for data processing and analysis.

Scientific transparency

The sources page distinguishes verified datasets, pending checks, missing resources and reference material. Regional selections represent bounding boxes rather than exact political boundaries. The displayed Theil–Sen slope interval does not correct for serial dependence, and statistical significance does not establish causation.

The game remains a prototype. Production input reliability and broader usability testing are outstanding validation work.
